23 But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed. 24 Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. 25 But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. 26 For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. (Galatians 3:23-26 KJV)

The “before faith came” is referring to the faith of Jesus Christ, as faith was manifested by Abraham long ago, but the saving faith of Jesus is what Paul is referring to. We were kept under the law, which essentially shut us up from being able to save ourselves, and made us look for a Savior to save us. The law was given to make sin come alive to us (Romans 7:9), and show us that we were, and are, unable to save ourselves, as our fallen human nature will not let us be holy enough to be saved (Romans 3:23). The Bible makes it clear that the law will judge those who are still under the law, by trying to earn from God. The law can save no one, as all have come short of fulfilling it completely. Therefore those who are still trying to earn their way to heaven, will not make it. You must be saved by putting faith in the Grace of God, not by works of the law (Romans 3:20).

This verse, as well as many others, shows that once the faith of Jesus has come, we are no longer under the law, and yet most churches try to preach the keeping of the law to be right with God. That is just not so, as the bible teaches us that our salvation is by the Grace of God, and not related to any works that we do, but only in our faith in Jesus Christ as our Savior. The reason the church teaches works as being necessary to please God, is to try to make us work for the church and Kingdom of God. If they would teach the love of God instead, they would get more service out of their members then they ever could by works. The good news of the Gospel is that we are saved by faith in Jesus Christ alone and the Grace of God that He brought to us, not anything we do (Romans 3:28).
